title: Resolving conflicts without panic
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read conflict markers, resolve a conflict deliberately, and back out of one entirely — so a conflict becomes a task rather than an emergency.

blocks.text: A conflict is Git telling you the truth: two people changed the same lines and it will not guess which one is right. It is not damage and nothing is lost. The panic comes from the markers looking alarming and from not knowing that you can always back out.

blocks.caption: What a conflict looks like
lines: Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

blocks.caption: Inside the conflicted file
lines: discount = 0.10        ← what the branch you are ON has
discount = 0.15        ← what the branch you are MERGING IN has

items: Everything between <<<<<<< and ======= is the receiving branch's version
Everything between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming version
Your job is to leave the file as it should actually be — and delete all three marker lines

blocks.title: The result is a decision, not a choice between two buttons
blocks.text: Often neither side is correct on its own. If one branch added validation and the other changed the same function's signature, the right answer is a version containing both. Editors offer 'accept ours / accept theirs' buttons that make this look binary; read what each side was for before clicking either.

blocks.caption: Same four steps every time
lines: git status                 # which files are conflicted
# open each one, edit it into the state it should be, remove the markers
git add pricing.py         # 'this file is resolved'
git status                 # repeat until nothing is unmerged
git commit                 # completes the merge (message is pre-filled)

blocks.title: You can always leave
blocks.text: git merge --abort returns everything to exactly how it was before you started, as long as you have not committed the merge. Knowing this is available is most of what turns a conflict from frightening into routine — you can try a resolution, decide it is wrong, and start again.

rows: The list of conflicted files — the only reliable to-do list
During a conflict, shows the conflicting regions specifically
Take the receiving branch's whole file
Take the incoming branch's whole file
Cancel the merge entirely and go back
The commits from both sides that touched this file

blocks.title: 'ours' and 'theirs' mean less than they sound like
blocks.text: During a merge, ours is the branch you are standing on and theirs is the branch arriving. During a rebase these are reversed, because the commits are being replayed onto the other side. When in doubt, read the file rather than trusting the words.

items: Merge the shared branch into yours regularly instead of once at the end — small differences conflict less than a month of divergence
Keep branches short-lived; a branch open for weeks is a conflict being written slowly
Split large files that everyone edits, when you can — the conflict is a symptom of the layout
Agree on formatting and enforce it automatically, so nobody's editor rewrites whole files

blocks.title: Create a conflict on purpose and resolve it
steps: In ~/git-lab: git switch main && echo 'price = 10' > pricing.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Set price to 10"
Run: git switch -c feature/price && echo 'price = 15' > pricing.txt && git commit -am "Raise price to 15"
Run: git switch main && echo 'price = 12' > pricing.txt && git commit -am "Raise price to 12"
Run: git merge feature/price        (CONFLICT — as designed)
Run: git merge --abort && cat pricing.txt   (everything is back)
Run: git merge feature/price        (again — now resolve it)
Edit pricing.txt to the value you want, delete the marker lines
Run: git add pricing.txt && git commit && git log --oneline --graph -5
blocks.expected: A conflict you caused deliberately, backed out of once, then resolved and completed. Having done it on purpose in a sandbox is what stops it being alarming the first time it happens on real work.

cheatsheet: A conflict means two changes touched the same lines — nothing is lost
<<<<<<< HEAD is the branch you are on · >>>>>>> is the branch arriving
Edit the file to what it should be, then delete all three marker lines
git add <file> marks it resolved · git commit completes the merge
git merge --abort returns everything to before the merge
The answer is often both sides combined, not one side chosen
ours/theirs swap meaning during a rebase — read the file, not the label
Merge the shared branch into yours often; long-lived branches breed conflicts

checkpoint.prompt: In a conflicted file, what is the section between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= ?

choices.C: The version from the branch you are currently on

checkpoint.explanation: HEAD is where you are standing. The section after ======= is what the arriving branch contains.

checkpoint.prompt: You start resolving a conflict and realise you do not have enough context. What is the safe move?

choices.B: Pick 'accept theirs' for every file and move on
choices.C: git merge --abort, then ask the author later

checkpoint.explanation: Abort restores the exact state from before the merge. Guessing at a resolution silently discards someone's intent, which is worse than delaying. Go back once you can ask the other author.

checkpoint.prompt: Which is true about resolving a conflict?

choices.A: Git can resolve it automatically with the right flag
choices.B: You must choose one side or the other
choices.D: The correct result is often a combination of both sides

checkpoint.explanation: Each was solving a different problem. Two people changed the same lines for different reasons. The resolution should preserve both intentions where they are compatible.

checkpoint.prompt: What most reliably reduces how often conflicts happen?

choices.B: Keeping branches short-lived and up to date
choices.D: Turning off automatic formatting, which causes most conflicts

checkpoint.explanation: Conflicts scale with divergence. A branch that stays close to the shared branch has little to conflict with; one that runs for a month accumulates the collision in advance. Up to date means merging the shared branch into yours regularly.
